tagline: Green River towns lead into the Everly family’s Muhlenberg County.
intro: The Everly Brothers Rock-N-Roll Trail connects Webster, McLean and Muhlenberg counties through a succession of state and U.S. highways. It reaches the Green River at Calhoun and passes through Central City, where the terrain includes rolling hills and steep bluffs along the river. The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet lists it as part of the Blues to Bluegrass Scenic Byway, designated January 29, 2004.

The name connects the drive to a musical family with roots in coal mining. Ike Everly worked in the mines from age 14; encouraged by his father to pursue music, he began singing with his wife, Margaret. Their son Don was born in Brownie in 1937, and that community eventually became part of Central City. In 1988, Central City began an Everly Brothers Homecoming to fund scholarships for county students.

From the Union County line, the route travels through Dixon and Sebree, then reaches Calhoun by way of Beech Grove. KY 81 carries it south through Sacramento and Bremen; US 431 continues through Central City. The final loop turns west on KY 176, north on KY 1380 and KY 189, then east on US 62 to the Ohio County line.

moments.title: Calhoun
moments.text: Calhoun began beside a difficulty in river travel: the Long Falls of the Green River. Henry Rhoads laid out the town in 1784–1785, and his brother Solomon built a fort to protect settlers and passage past the falls. In 1854, Calhoun defeated Rumsey, across the river, in the contest to become the new McLean County seat. The town occupies the north bank, with the Army Corps of Engineers’ Lock and Dam No. 2 on the river. KY 81 passes through town as Main Street. Across the water lies Rumsey, while KY 136 crosses Calhoun’s northern end.

moments.title: Sacramento
moments.text: Before it was Sacramento, this place was Crossroads, with a post office called Social Hill. George L. Helm platted and renamed the town in 1854. Local tradition holds that John Vickers suggested Sacramento after returning from the California Gold Rush. The road junction remains central to its geography: KY 81 and KY 85 meet in the northeastern part of town and separate just south of it. Main Street carries both routes through a town concentrated near their intersection with KY 254, or 2nd Street. KY 81 links Sacramento northward with Calhoun and southeastward with South Carrollton.

moments.title: Drakesboro
moments.text: Drakesboro gives four guitar players a shared memorial: the Four Legends Fountain, constructed in 1992. It honors Kennedy Jones, Ike Everly, Mose Rager and Merle Travis, pioneers of thumb picking who all have close ties to Muhlenberg County. Rager’s name also belongs to the road through town: KY 176 is Mose Rager Boulevard. The highway meets US 431 at the eastern reach of the municipal boundaries. That section of US 431 carries another musician’s name, John Prine. Ike Everly, remembered by the fountain, was a guitarist as well as the father of Don and Phil.
